human_tolerance.notes: Uses remote mountain and desert terrain; human activity can displace sheep from prime habitat.

phases.name: mating
phases.note: Northern and temperate U.S. populations usually rut in November and December; desert populations can peak earlier, so this calendar is regional and simplified.

phases.name: young
phases.note: Lambing: northern U.S. populations generally give birth late April through late June; desert populations differ.

taxonomy.note: GBIF match is exact, accepted, species rank, canonical name Ovis canadensis; authority Shaw, 1804.

external.note: Checked GBIF usageKey 2441119 and iNaturalist active taxon 42391 independently; both resolve to Ovis canadensis at species rank.

range.note: North American native range summarized as United States, Canada and Mexico; GBIF occurrence results for US are used only for activity support.

traits.body_plan.note: Four-limbed mammal; body-plan classification is the record's normalized mapping.

traits.locomotion_modes.note: Walking is observed while foraging; source also describes steep-terrain climbing. Trot and gallop are modeled hoofed-mammal gaits.

traits.nest_type.note: Ground, because lambs are born on steep lambing terrain and there is no nest structure.

traits.size_class.note: Large classification from adult mass ranges.

traits.mass_kg.note: Equal-sex average of the midpoints of the reported typical male range (58-143 kg) and female range (34-91 kg): ((58+143)/2 + (34+91)/2)/2 = 81.5 kg. This is a transparent display estimate, not a population-weighted mean.

traits.mass_range_kg.note: Envelope of reported typical adult female (34-91 kg) and male (58-143 kg) ranges.

traits.length_m.note: Equal-sex average of sex-specific range midpoints: male (1.6-1.85 m), female (1.28-1.58 m), yielding 1.58 m; display estimate, not population-weighted.

traits.shoulder_height_m.note: Equal-sex average of midpoints of male 0.90-1.05 m and female 0.75-0.90 m ranges = 0.90 m.

traits.lifespan_y.note: 12 years is the midpoint of the Forest Service species account typical wild lifespan of 10-14 years; FEIS further reports 10-12 as common among sheep surviving past age 8-9. This is a wild-life estimate, not captive longevity.

traits.diet.note: Authored allocation for the required model field: 0.7 graze and 0.3 browse. FEIS says grasses and forbs are primary, while browse varies by availability and is dominant for desert populations; the proportions are a coarse simulation judgement, not measured diet fractions.

traits.social.note: Group structure and broad 1-100 interval reflect solitary/bachelor rams and ewe nursery groups of 25-100; group composition varies by sex, season, and population.

traits.activity_pattern.note: The account describes mountain sheep as generally diurnal, with alternating feeding and resting bouts; it notes populations may feed after sunset.

traits.defense.note: Flee is a generalized threat response; rugged escape terrain is the species' key defense strategy.

traits.wariness.note: Authored judgement: remote, wary wild ungulate; account describes displacement by human activity.

habitat.use.note: Ground use from terrestrial mountain and desert habitat.

habitat.shelter_tag.note: Generic shelter stands for cliffs and rock outcrops, which the schema cannot express directly.

habitat.resources.note: Food weights follow the authored diet allocation; water and shelter presence are categorical habitat needs rather than intake shares.

habitat.human_tolerance.note: Avoider and gardens false reflect use of remote mountain/desert areas and documented displacement by human recreation and development.

seasonal.strategy.note: ActiveYearRound; sources describe seasonal range movements but no hibernation.

seasonal.phases.note: US- scoped temperate/northern rut and lambing windows from FEIS. Desert populations differ; a single calendar cannot represent them.

seasonal.life_stages.note: Juvenile duration to approximately the first year is a simulation simplification; lambs are precocious and develop rapidly.

behavior.note: Authored parameters for the shared ground-forager: graze resource, walk forage, gallop flee, and nighttime rest match a mostly diurnal feeding and bedding cycle. The flee/calm/food radii (45/60/80 m) are explicit simulation judgements because no source quantifies those interaction distances. The shared program has no climb action, so it cannot enact the species’ steep-cliff climbing; that capability remains an explicit behavior blocker for review.

look.note: Brown body coat and white rump patch follow the description; paired curled horns represent a ram. Block proportions and colors are authored visual approximations.

activity.US.note: United States country-level monthly observations. The curve is the mean of provider effort-corrected monthly shares; iNaturalist tier A has 2,217 observations and GBIF tier A has 4,139, all twelve months present. Observation frequency is an imperfect proxy for animal activity, and this national curve does not resolve regional or population differences.
